Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Non-profit Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Vignette:
Rajan had always thought of himself as someone who could handle things. For thirty years, he had managed budgets, coordinated volunteers, and kept the food bank’s operations running smoothly. But that evening in the storage room, after the last volunteer had left and the lights had been dimmed for the night, something ended that he had not known could be taken from him. The man had come from behind, a hand clamped over Rajan’s mouth, and he had felt a knee drive into the small of his back as he was forced against the metal shelving. The clatter of canned goods hitting the concrete floor, the sound of his own breath trapped against that palm, the sharp, tearing sensation in his lower abdomen that he would later learn was a pulled muscle from struggling—these details had not faded. When the memory returned now, and it returned many times each day, he heard that clatter of cans in his ears as clearly as if they were still falling. He felt that same tearing ache in his gut, a phantom pain that made him press his hand to his stomach and wince. And yet, when his therapist asked him to describe what had happened, he found himself mute. He knew the sequence of events perfectly, could replay them in his mind frame by frame, but the words to explain it to another person simply would not come. His mouth would go dry, and he would shake his head, unable to begin.

In the weeks that followed, Rajan had come to a quiet, devastating conclusion about himself. His reactions since that night—the way he had frozen, the way he had not fought back harder, the way he now jumped at every unexpected sound—proved to him that he was a lousy coper. Other people, he was certain, would have handled this better. Other people would not be reduced to a shaking mess by the sudden slam of a car door. He had also become convinced that he would never feel normal emotions again. The world had gone flat, as though someone had drained the color and warmth from every experience. He went through the motions at work, but he felt nothing—no satisfaction from a job well done, no pleasure in a colleague’s joke, no warmth from his daughter’s phone calls. And he was certain, with a bone-deep certainty, that he was now permanently an outsider. He sat alone in the break room during his shifts, watching his coworkers laugh and talk, and he knew that he was separated from them by a glass wall that would never come down. They lived in a world where bad things did not happen in storage rooms. He lived in a world where they did.

The world itself had become a place of constant threat. Rajan could no longer tolerate being alone in a room or a building. The silence pressed in on him, and he would find himself listening—not for anything specific, but for the sound of footsteps, the creak of a door, the whisper of fabric that might mean someone was entering his home. He kept his back to the wall at all times, whether in his office, in a restaurant, or in his own living room. He needed to see the entire room, every corner, every doorway. Unexpected sounds—a truck backfiring, a dropped tray in the cafeteria—sent a jolt through him that left his hands trembling. And touch had become unbearable. When a colleague touched his shoulder to get his attention, he flinched so violently that he knocked over a cup of coffee. The man had apologized, but Rajan had seen the confusion in his eyes, and the shame had burned in his chest for the rest of the day.

There were nights when the pressure inside him became too great, when the memories and the fear and the flat, grey emptiness built to a point where he thought he might burst. On those nights, alone in his apartment, he would hurt himself physically. A sharp pinch, a scratch from a key, a hard slap against his own thigh. The pain was a release valve. It was something real, something he could feel, something that cut through the numbness for a few seconds. He knew it was not a solution. He knew it was a sign that something was deeply wrong. But in those moments, it was the only thing that made the pressure stop.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was not his own suffering, but a phone call from his daughter. She had called to check on him, as she did every Sunday, and he had found himself unable to speak. The words would not come. He had sat there, the phone pressed to his ear, listening to her voice grow more and more worried, and he had felt nothing. No love, no guilt, no longing. Just that flat, grey emptiness. He had hung up without saying goodbye. That night, he had looked up a therapist’s number. He was not hoping to feel better. He did not believe that was possible. He was hoping, at best, to learn how to pretend well enough that his daughter would not have to worry about him anymore. But beneath that, buried so deep he could barely acknowledge it, was a small, frightened part of him that was afraid he would never come back from this—that the man in the storage room had taken more than he had realized, and that the person Rajan used to be was gone for good.
